segments.text: c1_V1-k1.1-kathamcit.md

The first sūtra of the ĪPK: "having in some way obtained (kathamcit āsādya) the Lord of the gods, [I make...]." The "in some way" is the hinge — it concedes that the attainment of the Lord does not come by a determinate, specifiable means, yet it is still an attainment. The commentary opens the epistemology: everything rests in consciousness (saṃvidviśrānti), and manifestation is non-different from the light (prakāśābhinnatva). The world does not stand over against a light that reveals it; it rests in consciousness and is one with the manifestation. This is where the IPVV's real doctrine begins.
c1_V1-k1.2-drstapi.md

The kārikā: the Self is "seen yet unperceived" (dṛṣṭo'py anupalakṣitaḥ) — it is present, but not perceived as an object among objects. The example is the pot: the pot that stands before me is seen, though I may not notice it; its non-recognition does not mean it is absent. So with the Self — it is always present, always "seen" in the sense of being the very awareness of all seeing, yet it is not singled out as an object. Non-recognition is not absence. This is the recognition-thesis in seed: the Self is always there, and what is lacking is not its presence but the recognition of it.
c1_V1-k1.3-atmaiva.md

The kārikā: the own-self alone is the Lord (ātmaiva īśvaraḥ). This is the maximal claim of the recognition-thesis, stated in its root form — not that the self is like the Lord, or participates in the Lord, but that the own-self *is* the Lord. The commentary develops the corollary that the self has the power of knowledge and action (jñāna-kriyā-śakti), and draws the line of the dvairāśya — the division into the inert and the non-inert, with the self squarely on the side of the non-inert consciousness that knows and acts. This is the seed of the whole account of the powers.
c1_V1-k1.4-1.5-buddhipurva.md

The kārikās 1.4–1.5 treat two connected claims: the inference of other minds and the self-luminosity of cognition, against the Naiyāyika. Cognition is not a quality that the self acquires from an object through a separate means; it is self-luminous — it manifests both its object and itself in a single act. From this it follows that other cognitions are not inferred by connecting a perceived sign to an unperceived quality (as the Naiyāyika's inference-theory would have it); they are manifest as self-luminous in their own right. The rejection of the Naiyāyika's theory of cognition as a derived quality is what opens the way to the self-cognition account.
c1_V1-purvapaksa-k1.2.7-citsvarupam.md

The kārikā: knowledge is of the nature of consciousness (jñānaṃ citsvarūpam). Against the Vaiśeṣika/Nyāya view that knowledge is a quality produced in the self by its contact with an object, Abhinavagupta holds that knowledge is consciousness-natured — it is self-luminous, manifesting both the object and itself. This is the root of the two claims that follow: the cognition cannot be reduced to an inert quality (V1-G), and it is ultimately self-cognition (V1-K). The kārikā states the positive essence from which the refutations proceed.
c1_V1-purvapaksa-opening.md

The second vimarśa opens with a homage to Bhairava as the wave of his own power, and then announces the structure of the pūrvapakṣa: seven verses (satyaṃ kintu ... smṛtyapohanaśaktimān) examining the impossibility of the rival views (paradarśanānupapatti) — the refutation of the Buddhist and Sāṃkhya positions on the self and its lordship. The homage establishes the doctrinal frame: the argument that follows is conducted from the standpoint of the self-aware Lord, whose power is the wave of his own manifestation. The seven verses lay out the plan of the refutation.
c1_V1-purvapaksa-smrtibhranti-sankaranandana.md

The passage engages the memory-error (smṛti-bhrānti) and the philosopher Bhaṭṭa Śaṅkaranandana, who presses the memory-argument. The Buddhist opponent points to cases where memory goes wrong — where we misremember, or remember what we did not experience — and argues these show memory cannot be a reliable guide to a persisting self. Abhinavagupta's reply is that even the error presupposes the structure memory requires: to misremember is still to appropriate a past experience as one's own, and that appropriation requires a persisting recognizer. The error-cases confirm, rather than refute, the self that memory presupposes.
c1_V1-upoddhata-k1-2-ahampratiti.md

The upoddhāta faces the Buddhist account of the "I." On the Buddhist view the "I"-cognition (ahaṃ-pratīti) is tied to the body: the sense of self arises as a construction bound to the bodily complex, and is therefore as perishable and as constructed as the body itself. Abhinavagupta's counter-position, which this passage sets up, is that the "I"-recollection is not so confined — it points to a self-awareness that underlies the body-bound construction rather than being produced by it. The distinction between the body-bound "I"-cognition (which the Buddhist can explain) and the reflexive "I"-grasp (which he cannot) is the pivot of the whole refutation.
c1_V1-upoddhata-k11-karta.md

The upoddhāta k11 closes the pūrvapakṣa with the strongest conclusion of the no-self attack: "thence the agent too is constructed" (tena kartāpi kalpitaḥ). If the self, the cognition, the action, and the relation have all been shown to be impossible, then the agent — the one who is supposed to act — is likewise only a construction, a useful fiction with no underlying reality. This is the Buddhist conclusion in its fullest form. The siddhānta will reverse it entirely: the agent is not a construction but the real, free self, whose lordship the recognition restores.
c1_V1-upoddhata-k3-memory.md

The upoddhāta's third kārikā makes the memory-argument for the eternal self. Memory reaches what one has experienced; but if the self were momentary (as the kṣaṇikavāda holds), no experience could be carried across moments to be remembered, and memory would be impossible. The fact that memory occurs — that I can re-appropriate a past experience as mine — shows there is a self that persists through the change of moments. The argument is the same as in the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi: memory presupposes a persisting recognizer, and that recognizer is the non-inert self.
c1_V1-upoddhata-k4-5-antargadu.md

The upoddhāta k4–5 develop the memory-argument against the impression-theory. If memory is from an impression (saṃskāra) — a trace left by the experience — then the objector asks how a trace can survive when there is no persisting subject to hold it; the image is the "stone in the belly" (antargaḍu), something carried without being digested or integrated. Abhinavagupta's reply: the impression-theory alone cannot explain memory, because an impression is only a trace of content, and the re-appropriation of that content as "mine" requires a persisting self. The impression-theory thus presupposes the very subject it was meant to replace.
c1_V1-upoddhata-k6-k8-caitanyamajada.md

The upoddhāta k6 & k8 state the core claim: consciousness (caitanya) is ajaḍā — non-inert, not a passive thing. The seed of the crystal-argument (IPK 1.5.11): a consciousness that merely reflected objects without knowing that it reflected them would be no different from a crystal — it would show, but be inert. What distinguishes consciousness from the inert is that it is aware of itself in the very act of manifesting. The claim grounds the whole refusal to treat consciousness as a product of inert matter, and it is the same argument the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi develops at length.
c1_V1-upoddhata-k9-10-sambandha.md

The upoddhāta k9–10 argue that action is not a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa). A pramāṇa yields a cognition of an object; action yields a change in the world, not a cognition. And the only genuine relation between things is the cause-effect relation — the relation by which one thing produces another. This is the ground for the later account (V3-G/I) that causality is the conscious knower's agency: because the only real relation is causal, and causation is an act of a conscious agent, the world's structure is the structure of agency, not of inert connection.
c1_V1-upoddhata-mangala.md

The opening homage to Bhairava as the Heart (hṛdaya). The Heart is "not sundered from the triad of the powers" (śakti-tritaya) — the powers of will, knowledge, and action are not separate faculties added to consciousness but its own indivisible activity. It bears the reflexion-fill (bhāvana-nibhṛta) and the upsurge of the unfolding, and it becomes the all-formed (viśvarūpa) — the entire world is the Heart's own form, not something external to it. The homage establishes the whole frame of the work: the reality to be expounded is the self-aware Heart that is the world.  The commentary then draws the first doctrinal consequence: everything rests in consciousness (saṃvidviśrānti), and manifestation is non-different from the light (prakāśābhinnatva). Nothing stands outside the light; to be is to be manifested in it. This is the seed of the entire nondual epistemology.
c1_V1A-svatyandya.md

The very opening of the IPVV. The maṅgala has been made; now Abhinavagupta expounds the first kārikā — the spontaneity (svācchandya) of the Lord. The blue and the other things, without abandoning their blue-ness, shine forth and are one with the manifestation (prakāśābhedamayāḥ). This is the Lord's spontaneity: being of the nature of consciousness, he shines as the varied knowers and knowns, with a body that appears as more than the consciousness-form even though it is not more — and he is aware of this (vimṛśati). The image is the mirror: the mirror reflects the wall, the house, the elephant, the horse, the person, the pot, the potter — all the distinctions — without being more than its own surface. But the mirror does not know that it reflects; its not being aware is its inertia (jaḍatva). The param-eśvara, shining thus, *is* aware of himself as shining.  The time-objection — "then it would always shine so" — is answered: the "always" (śaśvat) has no independent time against which it could fail; "at this time" means nothing other than the sun's movement. There is no time outside the light. Hence the four epithets: śaśvat (un-cut by time), acchanna (never other than its own form), svaccha (clear — able to appear as more while being only itself), svacchanda (spontaneous — resting in its own freedom). The prostration is the entry (samāveśa) into this self-aware Śiva.
c1_V1B-eligibility.md

The commentary on "having attained, in some way" (kathaṃcit) opens up what the prostration is and who is eligible to make it. The prostration is *two-resting*: it must, being conveyed through one of the two [the Lord and the devotee], culminate in the rest of both. The "jaya" words, moved by the Lord's excess, must have the self-subordinating as their support; the "namaḥ" words, moved by the self-subordinating re-recollection, must rest in the Lord's excess. The two are one thing, two-aspect.  The attainment of the Lord is the attainment of servant-ness (dāsya), and the servant-ness is the heart of the eligibility. The four Gītā-devotees — the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, the knower — are all eligible, in their gradations, for the dāsya and the recognition. The "kathaṃcit" (in some way) says the dāsya is extremely hard to get; the more is the self-subordination stated.
c1_V1C-svatma.md

The kārikā says "the own-self alone" (svātmā eva) is the Lord. The objection presses on what "own-self" includes: if the maheśvara is the self of the blue, he is equally the self of the yellow — so how is the world divided? Abhinavagupta answers that the "own" (sva) is not restricted; the whole being-class, inert and conscious, is related. For the inert, in their inert-ness, even being/non-being is hard in the self: "it shines for me, for Caitra" fails, since the perception belongs to the perceiver. Without the blue's being-manifested there is no own-life; so the blue and the rest are awareness-forms (bodhātmānaḥ), and their own-self too is the maheśvara.  The division of the world is then answered: all the known is the *body* (śarīra) of the consciousness-self. As the body, though known, is "I," so the whole world is "I" to the consciousness. The division is of what appears within that consciousness, not a division of the self itself.
c1_V1D-memory-eternal-knower.md

The objection is the Rāmāyaṇa: memory reaches only the experienced, and "I was not at the time of the Rāmāyaṇa." Abhinavagupta answers that the param-essence knower — the consciousness-self — is un-cut by all three times; the "I" that was not then is only the present body, not the self. Memory itself presupposes the prior experience, and the prior experience presupposes the knower who was there.  The self's manifestation is not un-precedented (apūrva); the knower's appearing-as-new presupposes the prior knower. The param-essence knower is never un-precedented; all the knowers are un-divided from him, so in truth there is no un-precedented appearing. The Gītā confirms it: "for truly I was never not."
c1_V1E-foregrounding.md

The question is what a valid means does here at all. A pramāṇa is supposed to establish what is not yet established; but the self is already the Lord, so a pramāṇa for it seems idle. Abhinavagupta's reply is that the pramāṇa does not establish a new thing — it foregrounds what is already present but hidden. Recognition does not bring the Lord into being; it brings the Lord, who was always present, into the foreground of awareness. The self moves from the background — an instrument lost among the things of the body and the world — to the primary thing seen. Nothing in the content changes; what changes is where the self stands.  The passage does not by itself establish that the self is ontologically the Lord; that claim is argued elsewhere. Its point here is narrower: it gives recognition a mechanism (foregrounding), so that the recognition-thesis does not collapse into either adding a new fact or doing nothing.
c1_V1F-upoddhata-opponents.md

The upoddhāta (the preliminary) faces the opponents who deny the self's lordship. The Cārvāka (materialist) cannot even frame a refutation, having no means of proof; the Sāṃkhya (the many selfs, or one self with hidden lordship) is not wholly far. The real pūrvapakṣin is the Buddhist (Sautrāntika/Vijñānavādin), who denies the self outright. Against him Abhinavagupta must establish that the self is the Lord.  The Cārvāka, lacking a stance of their own, cannot refute the other side without entering the means- of-proof conventions, in which they lose their Cārvāka-ness. So the Sautrāntika is the pūrvapakṣin here; those who accept the self — the many or the one with hidden lordship — are nearer.
c1_V1G-cognition-refuted.md

The Buddhist denied the self. But even granting the self, the opponent offered a reason for its lordship: "by the union of knowledge and action" (jñānakriyāyogāt). To refute this, Abhinavagupta shows that knowledge itself, as the opponent conceives it, is impossible — whether it is taken as of the consciousness-form (then it is eternal, like the self, and cannot be a momentary quality) or as inert (then it cannot reveal anything).  The refutation is by prasaṅga (the undesired consequence): by the same reason by which the self is eternal, the cognition too would be eternal; but then, being so, it could not be a quality. The cognition is un-established in the opponent's view on either horn.
c1_V1H-enjoyment-reflection.md

What is enjoyment (bhoga) — the experiencing of objects? Abhinavagupta argues it is the *union of reflections* in the consciousness: the reflection of consciousness (cit-pratibimba) and the reflection of the object (viṣaya-pratibimba) meet in the buddhi, joined by the ahaṅkāra into the single "I know this." Against the Vaiśeṣika, who makes the cognition a quality of the self joined by inherence (samavāya), Abhinava shows the union is not real.  The self is consciousness-mere; it is not the enjoyer of objects. The ahaṅkāra (the ego) makes the self — which is not in itself an enjoyer — dealt with as an enjoyer. In the metaphor there is no real change in the thing-metaphored.
c1_V1I-action-refuted.md

Having shown the cognition is impossible in the opponent's view, Abhinavagupta now shows action (kriyā) is impossible too. Kārikā 9: the action of a body is the coming-to-be of this and that place-and-the-rest; it is not other, from the unseen (adṛṣṭa); nor is it one — for the ordered (the sequence) of the one is not fit. One action cannot be at once this place and that; a single action could not produce the ordered succession.
c1_V1J-agent-constructed.md

The Buddhist's pūrvapakṣa has denied the self, the cognition, and the action. Now it completes itself: since the relation (between cognition and object, or agent and action) is also impossible, "thence the agent too is constructed" (kartāpi kalpitaḥ). The "thence" gathers a fourfold absence: the absence of the action, the absence of the object, the absence of the relation, and the absence of the determination of the being. The relation is not, for the two-resting thing cannot be one; hence the agent, like everything else, is only a construction. This is the close of the no-self attack.
c1_V1K-siddhanta-svasamvid.md

The Buddhist's pūrvapakṣa has denied the self, the cognition, the action, and the relation. Now the siddhānta replies, and its first move is a striking concession-and-appropriation. Abhinavagupta grants the Buddhist that the cognition is not a separate thing standing over against a self in the Sāṃkhya/Kāṇāda manner — it is not a quality of a distinct subject. But he turns this to his own end: because the cognition is not a separate quality, it is *self-cognition* (svasaṃvid). The cognition manifests itself in the very act of manifesting its object. And this self-cognition is precisely the self the Buddhist denied. The "I"-seeing (dṛk) is self-luminous, and it is the Lord.  The move is decisive: the Buddhist's rejection of a separate self is accepted, and the self-awareness that remains is identified as the true self. What the Buddhist took for the death of the self turns out to be its recognition.
c1_V1L-yogipratyaksa.md

If the self is not manifest as an object, how does the yogin perceive another's cognition clearly? Abhinavagupta answers: this is the yogipratyakṣa — the yogin's *perception*, not an inference. By the discipline (the holding, the meditating, the samādhi) one comes, in the union with the other, to meditate the non-difference of the self from the other; and that meditation, following the truth of the thing, makes the other's cognition shine forth directly. In that act the self that sees and the self that are seen are one.
c1_V1M-determination.md

The Buddhist's last resort is the *determination* (adhyavasāya) — the act by which the cognition is taken to establish an external thing. Abhinavagupta shows it cannot. The external-object-made is only by the strength of the firm-practice-impression (dṛḍhābhyāsavāsanā); from the very first the appearance is drawn-to-the-external only for the slow-minded. He who knows the cause of the appearance does not determine its externality at all.  The determination is error-form: it cannot establish on either side — the inert part cannot establish, and the non-inert part (the pure self-experience) is un-divided from the memory-cognition, not external-natured.
c1_V1N-close-mahesvara.md

The cognitions are of the manifestation-mere own-form. How, then, do they not take the form of the "I" when they shine beyond the "I"-part? Their excess over the "I"-part — the non-pervasion, the non-eternity — is made by the object-facing upādhi. The māyā is the Lord's power, which does not cover his own form; and the synthesis (anusandhāna) is the consciousness alone. The maheśvara's śaktis — knowledge, memory, apoha — are his. The colophon closes the volume.
c1_V2A-memory-lords-power.md

The passage rejects the ordinary account of memory as the revival of a past impression — a trace stirred up after the experience has gone. Abhinavagupta replaces it with a positive claim: memory is itself a knowledge, the Lord's own power, the un-broken manifestation by which the past and the present are held together in a single "I." The "I" shines in two directions — as the seer of the blue (inward) and as "I, thus" (outward). By the freedom of the awareness one first construes within "I would see the blue," and then the blue appears without. When we say "the jar stands, will stand, stood," what makes this possible is the un-brokenness of the manifestation — the awareness that holds the jar's appearances together across the moments. The experience is the gate through which time is entered.  The passage establishes that memory is the un-broken manifestation, not an impression's revival. It does not by itself establish every stronger claim about the eternal self; that argument is developed with the preceding and following material.
c1_V2B-pastness-svasamvitti.md

How, if the manifestation has no touch of time, do we remember yesterday? The pastness is not a real quality of the object; it is the *being-previously-manifested*. The one light, contracting under the upādhis of place and time ("yesterday, thirsty, with that friend"), appears as the past. Memory is the re-apprehension of what was previously manifested.  The yogin, by the discipline, thins the body and the other's cognition shines in its own place. And the deepest point: cognition is self-cognition (svasaṃvitti) — self-luminous, distinguishing it from the inert — and because it is self-cognition, it is free to manifest the other.
c1_V2C-ajadapramatr.md

The yogin knows another's cognition. But a cognition can never be the *object* of another cognition — for the two would have to stand in the relation of object and holder. Abhinavagupta analyzes what "being an object" means: a thing is an object when the awareness assimilates its form (the sārūpya), which requires the object to be both like and unlike the cognition. But a cognition has no such difference from another: their form is the self-luminous awareness, which has nothing in it to be set over against another awareness. Two mirrors can reflect one another; two cognitions cannot.  The cognition is self-luminous, never made the object of another — the knower is the ajaḍa, the not-inert. This establishes the conscious knower, with which the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi closes.
c1_V2D-jnanasakti.md

The jñānaśakti (the knowledge-power) is the capacity by which anything is known. Its central claim: the manifestation is the very form of the objects. Their being *is* their being-manifested; to know a thing is to be the light in which it appears. The Vijñānavādin agrees the object is not outside but draws the wrong conclusion (no object at all). Abhinava replies: the inner blue-form is a reflection, and a reflection expects a ground — so the object is real as the ground of the manifestation.  The essence of the manifestation is the reflexive-awareness: the light that knows itself in knowing the object.
c1_V2E-external-inferred.md

The Vijñānavādin grants the cognition is self-luminous but presses its inner form: the blue-form is a reflection, and a reflection demands a ground (the arpaka). The classic objection — how can you infer an external never perceived? — is answered with the sense-organ analogy: the sense-organ is never perceived, yet inferred as the cause of its perceptions. So too the external, inferred by the sārūpya (the conformity).  Even the determination "I see this object," though it begins as error, is by its bond to the thing a valid means: "even the error, being a relation, is a pramā" (bhrāntirapi saṃbandhaḥ pramā). The inference's own work is the sasaṃvāda — it confirms that the ground of the form is the thing, not that it creates the object.
c1_V2F-other-minds.md

The Buddhist hopes to infer another's mind — from Maitra's speech, the other stream. Abhinavagupta shows it cannot work. To infer the fire in the sandalwood from the smoke, you must set aside the sandalwood's fragrance; to infer another's mind, you would need the further distinction — the "being-gone-to-the-other," that this utterance belongs to Maitra and not to you — which cannot be inferred from the mere utterance. And only the *aimed* action is the wish's effect; from the mere utterance one cannot infer the wish.  The other-stream cannot be inferred. And then the positive turn: "the appearances alone suffice" (kārikā 6) — the ābhāsa is real and enough; the external (whole or atom) is needless.
c1_V2G-dream-inversion.md

The external object has been shown to be un-establishable — neither as a whole nor as atoms. The objector asks how this is so, since the external was earlier inferred from the variety of the appearance-order. Abhinavagupta answers with the īśvarādvaya: the external is not needed, because the Lord manifests the whole world from within himself, by his own will, without an external material cause — as a yogin does. The decisive image is the dream. The Buddhist had used the dream to prove the world's unreality (it appears without a cause). Abhinavagupta accepts that the dream is uncaused, but draws the opposite conclusion: the dream shows that consciousness alone can create an object-mass by its will.  The passage establishes the īśvarādvaya — the Lord manifests from within. Whether this yields one universal creator, rather than a creating consciousness, is a further claim addressed later.
c1_V2H-vimarsa-paravak.md

The claim is that the essence of light is the reflexive awareness, not the bare showing of objects. The crystal supplies the contrast: a light that merely showed the world without knowing that it showed it would be no different from crystal — it would reflect, but be inert. What makes the light conscious is the self-awareness in the very act of manifesting. The passage then identifies this self-knowing with the supreme speech (parā-vāk) and with the Lord's freedom and lordship.  The identification with the Word is the extension: the reflexivity is not a bare self-presence but the supreme speech from which the lower levels of language descend. This is why the word-joined "I" need not be a construction — language is the form the self-grasp takes, not something that produces it. The passage establishes the reflexivity claim; the full account of the powers and the Lordship is developed in the following vimarśas.
c1_V2I-sphuratta.md

The grammarian would make speech, the paśyantī, a separate supreme principle. But speech and the mind are only the operation of the ego — like the hand; none is the param. The param-eśvara is the word-mass (śabdarāśi). The throbbing (sphurattā) — the very pulsing of the manifestation — is the great being, undivided by place and time, the heart of the param-Lord (kārikā 14); it is the same as the spanda, the wave.  The powers by which the Lord acts — the making of the known (jñeyīkaraṇa), the determination (adhyavasāya) — are all the reflexive-awareness, contracted by the māyā-power into the many forms (kārikā 18).
c1_V2J-samskara.md

What makes an experience strong enough to lay the seed of memory? It is the resting of the experience in the reflexive-awareness — the moment it is aware of itself, "I, thus, shine." Without that, the experience would be an inert flash; it could not lay a seed nor be awakened. The Bhaṭṭa said the strength lays the seed; but even this strength is the resting in the knower. The coconut-island dweller, who never saw smoke, does not remember fire from smoke — without the vimarśa-form cause, the impression is neither laid nor awakened.  And the determination "this jar" is itself the reflexive-awareness: beyond name and form, the param-Lord's power manifesting like the self, not by the this-ness (kārikā 20).
c1_V2K-vacakasphota.md

When we say "this jar," the word is not pasted onto a free-standing thing; it is superimposed on the meaning (adhyāsa). If the word were not superimposed, it would be recalled as a bare sound — "from this fire, ḍhak" — not as the speaker of a meaning. The word, being itself a manifestation, has the reflexive-awareness; it is self-luminous, like a lamp that reveals the objects and itself.  And the order of cognition, memory, determination is only by the place-and-time of the *different cognized* objects; in themselves, the reflexive-awareness-resting cognitions are one and order-less (kārikā 21).
c1_V2L-nonconstructed-I.md

The objection is straightforward: if reflexive awareness is joined to linguistic form, why is it not simply a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? Abhinavagupta answers by asking what construction actually does. The forms considered involve combining, differentiating, or determining contents. The awareness expressed as "I," however, is not treated as one more relation constructed between independently given elements. The point is therefore not merely that the "I" is linguistically unusual; it is that linguistic articulation does not show that the underlying self-awareness is itself produced by conceptual determination. This allows Abhinavagupta to preserve a distinction between reflexive self-awareness and the conceptual operations that articulate it.  The stronger Śaiva conclusion — that this self-awareness belongs ultimately to a single universal subject — is not established by this passage alone and depends on arguments elsewhere.
c1_V2M-descent-states.md

The consciousness descends, step by step, into the forms of the world — the void, the breath, the intellect, the body — and with each descent the self-conceit sinks further (the elephant in the mud-bank). The prāṇa is first for the world; the consciousness-tattva presides over it, which presides over the intellect, the puryaṣṭaka, and the body. As the Gītā says, the Lord goes from body to body through the prāṇa-puryaṣṭaka, as the wind carries the scents.  The construction (vikalpa, kārikā 6) is the joining of the "this" from the prior appearance; but the continuity (anusandhāna) — the self through all the states, from life to life — is not a construction; it is the one consciousness. In the dealing (kārikā 7) the Lord manifests the inner object-mass without by the will — the kṛtyapañcaka, the fivefold work.
c1_V2N-inner-appearance.md

The inner appearance — the self-grasp, the reflexive-awareness — stands firm in memory, in construction, and in cognition alike (kārikā 8). It is not something that flickers in and out; it is the one light that runs through them all. It is innate in the external-form cognition (kārikā 9), in the freely-wandering construction (kārikā 10), and from its manifestation knowledge and action are clear for every living one (kārikā 11). Even in liberation the freed souls are distinct, yet their manifestation is the un-broken all-knowing. The inner appearance never fails.
c1_V2O-orderless-support.md

The powers — knowledge, memory, removal — have been established. But a power needs a support, and the question is what supports them. Kārikā 1 gives the support's own form in the image of the pratibhā: the flashing that runs through the ordered word-objects, seasoned with their order, touched by it — but itself not ordered. Its support is therefore not anything ordered, but the order-less, infinite-consciousness-form knower. And that knower is the great Lord.  The point of kārikā 1 is to establish that the support has this form — order-less, conscious, free — before the following verses prove that it exists by presence-and-absence. The passage does not by itself prove that all such order-less supports are numerically one; the unity is argued later.
c1_V2P-pramatr-vyapara.md

The valid means (pramāṇa) is not a separate instrument over against the knower; it is the knower's own operation (pramātṛ-vyāpāra). The five objects of perception and non-perception, thrown into the one consciousness-ocean, are joined by the freedom-wave; the one appearance is the cause-and-effect appearance; and the re-recollection is the knower's operation. As the Mukuta-saṃhitā says, the joiner alone is the means.  In memory (kārikā 5), that very self-consciousness is the valid means — "that alone, not another." Memory does not bring a new thing; it re-grasps what was already grasped. The memory is the prior experience, self-conscious, remembered.
c1_V2Q-omniscient.md

The saptamo vimarśa closes with the figure of the omniscient. Suppose there is a piśāca (goblin) in the dark interval; we do not see it, but the omniscient sees its atoms — no different from the atoms of the darkness. If the piśāca is truly absent, the omniscient sees only the atoms of light (āloka), and these are the ground of his dealing "there is no piśāca here." Whatever is, the omniscient sees it; so if in that place he does not see the piśāca, it is not there. His non-perception establishes; the limited seer's (the arvāk's) does not.
c1_V2R-mahesvarya.md

The great-Lordship (māheśvarya) is twofold — directed at objects of knowledge and at objects of action; here the knowledge-directed lordship is determined. The jñāna is the self-experience "aham" contracted by the tint of the self-splitting appearance. And the lordship is the *freedom in the appearance-group* (kārikā 1): the appearances are not all alike — some depend on the eye's co-presence at that time, others appear in the blind, in the darkness. The varied dealing is not caused by something outside the Lord; it is his freedom in the appearance-group.
c1_V2S-unity-mahesvarya.md

The passage closes the jñānādhikāra with the unity of the knowers. Kārikā 10: the whole dealing of the world — the path by which consciousnesses know, remember, and act together — would be impossible if the consciousnesses were mutually opaque streams; but the dealing is, so the consciousnesses must be one. The unity is argued via the dealing, not by a bare assertion of identity. The Sāṃkhya's separate puruṣa is then re-read: it is not another self but the un-recognized own-lordship, the contracted consciousness.  Kārikā 11 draws the conclusion: the great-Lordship is nothing but the reflexive awareness. The Lordship is not a fifth power added to the four; it is what the four are. The powers reduce to the self-awareness, and the self-awareness is the Lord.  The passage argues the unity via the dealing and identifies the Lordship with the self-awareness. It does not by itself establish the identity of all supports by the felt alone; that is a further claim.
c1_V3A-timeless-order.md

The kriyādhikāra opens a paradox: the Lord is beyond time and sequence, yet the world is shot through with sequence. How can the timeless act in time? The homage answers: Śiva, "though free of sequence, manifests manifold sequences." The image is the mirror: a mirror bears countless reflections without ceasing to be the one, undivided mirror. So the one consciousness can take up seemingly contradictory forms without its oneness being divided. This is the action-support (kriyāśraya): the one that acts is one, and because it is one it can show sequence at all.
c1_V3B-bhedabheda.md

The cognitions of action, relation, universal, substance, direction and time have a substrate that is at once one and many, and they are accepted as true — true by their stability and true by their efficacy. The example: the body of Caitra — and of Maitra — although it differs by place, time, and shape, shines forth without abandoning its oneness, in the recognition "this is the very same body." That unity is the action, in the judgment "Caitra is walking." The substrate is both one (the unity of the recognition) and many (the differences) — the bhedābheda.
c1_V3C-one-light.md

The passage asks what really makes a cognition valid. Ordinary discourse appears to locate the validating force in the object itself: a cognition of blue is stable because the blue object determines it. Abhinavagupta argues that this cannot be sufficient. If the object possessed this determining force simply in itself, its appearance would not be restricted to one subject rather than another. Its manifestation therefore depends upon consciousness. He then pushes the argument further: knower, means of knowledge, and known object are not ultimately three independently functioning factors, but aspects of a single manifestation or "light." The point of the passage is thus to relocate the operation of *pramāṇa* from an independently existing object to the event of manifestation itself.  The exact account of how this single manifestation becomes restricted to particular knowers is developed in the following discussion.
c1_V3D-synthesis.md

If the valid means seizes only an appearance, how can it reach the single thing those appearances belong to? The answer is the *synthesizing awareness* (anusandhāna) — the one reflective grasp that gathers the many appearances into one. The jar is divided by viewpoint, wish, and convention — long, round, upright, a being, a substance, a jar — yet the synthesis keeps it one. And the object-action makes a thing real: separate lamp-lights, gathered in one house, do one thing (they make it bright); streams, falling into the ocean, do one thing. The doer of one object-action must be one.
c1_V3E-error.md

If the means seizes only appearances, how do we tell true from false — the real jar from the illusory double-moon or the shell-mistaken-for-silver? Abhinavagupta's answer: error is a matter of the reflexive-awareness; the distinction is made not by the pramāṇa's being un-contradicted but by the *reflexive-awareness'* being un-contradicted. The thing I saw far off as a whole, I now see near with its details; it is one by the one recognition "this is the very thing I saw before." The shell-silver has no standing as the real silver. In the end it is the knower who is the ground of everything.
c1_V3F-grace.md

The vimarśa closes on how one attains the Lord: by the Lord's grace, through a fourfold effort — the initiatory rite (dīkṣā), the vision-yoga (dhyāna), knowledge (jñāna), and devotion (bhāvanā). The order matters: knowledge is preceded by initiation; and if one has not practiced the vision-yoga, there is devotion. And the prāṇa's being felt as "I" is not a conflict with the param-ātman — the two are present together; the param-ātman shines freely, and by that shining the prāṇa appears as "I."
c1_V3G-causality.md

The relation between the known and the knower has been shown to be the expansion of the action-power. Now Abhinavagupta turns to cause and effect: the essence of cause and effect is nothing but the relation of agent and object of action. Causality is the agency of a conscious knower. The Lord manifests the world by his will — the un-divided, un-ordered will tinted by the particular thing to be made. And the inert cannot cause: the seed cannot endow the sprout with being (it is either existent, and nothing is acquired, or non-existent, and cannot come to be). The potter creates the pot by his power; the yogin by his will alone.
c1_V3H-inference-across-knowers.md

The Vijñānavādin objects: if everything is appearance, cause and effect are only relations between appearances, and an un-manifested fire is nothing — so how can the smoke arise from it and be inferred? Abhinavagupta answers with the one creation: the Lord creates the appearances *for all the knowers at once, as one*. So the pervasion (smoke implies fire) belongs to every knower alike; the fire-appearance, indirect to the one who infers, is the "cause of the Lord" (adhipatipratyaya). Inference holds across knowers because the appearances are created as one. And the dependence of cause and effect is not a real otherness: the fire and its heat are one, joined by the synthesis.
c1_V3I-difference-real.md

The sharpest objection to the unity: if consciousness is one and the difference of things is mere ignorance, how is action possible? For action needs an agent and an object, distinct; but if all is one, there is no distinct object. Abhinavagupta first answers with the will-to-do — the single re-recollection marked by the will that joins the agent and the object.  Then he challenges the premise that the difference is ignorance. If the difference were an "un-explainable" ignorance, of whom would it be? The one-form reality cannot have an ignorance that presupposes a duality to be absent from; the separate souls cannot bear it, since they are supposed to be produced by it; and "un-explainable" is a refusal to answer, not an answer. The difference is real: cognition rests in difference as it does not rest in non-difference.  The passage establishes that the difference cannot be an un-explainable ignorance. The full positive account of the difference (as the self's own manifestation) is developed elsewhere.
c1_V3J-agama-sivatattva.md

The kriyādhikāra showed that the action-power's form is the un-clouded manifestation of all the categories. But what are these categories, the tattvas? Perception is not an omniscient eye; inference lacks the pervasion that would reach everything. Only the āgama — the revealed teaching — can measure the whole. And at the heart of it is the Śivatattva, the body of every category: cause-effect rests not in the inert but in the consciousness-form, whose essence is manifestation-and-reflexive-awareness. Knowledge and action — manifestation and reflexivity — are inseparable; this pair is the supreme form of all beings.
c1_V3K-kancukas.md

Descending to the bound knower, the pure self is covered by the kañcukas (the "armours"): niyati (fixity), kāla (time), rāga (attachment), vidyā (limited knowledge), kalā (limited agency). Take niyati: the seed is the cause of the sprout, not of the pot — the apparent fixing of each effect to its own cause. But this fixity belongs to the knower, not the known; in reality the Lord alone shines forth as "this is the cause of that," and the binding is a covering laid over the reality by the limited knower. The bound knower is the māyīya knower, facing the distinct things of the world, which are counted as twenty-three categories of the known.
c1_V3L-knowers-malas.md

The dvitīyo vimarśa examines the knowers, for the recognition of the Lord in the self is the heart of the śāstra. The homage is to the one "who wields the trident, cutting the three nooses" — the three stains (mala): āṇava (finitude), māyīya (objectivity), kārma (action). The bound knower, the paśu, is blind by māyā, wandering in saṃsāra, bound by his actions; he has lost the freedom of the awareness. Over against him stands the pati, the Lord, whose own-members are his own.
c1_V3M-states.md

The bound knower lives in a round of states. At the lowest extreme is the void: the pralayākala, the dissolved knower, with only the barest trace of an "I" — a sleep without a dream. With the breath come the three great states: deep sleep (suṣupta, with the vidyākalā / pralayākala grades), the dream (svapna, the mind's own making, refuted by the waking), and waking (jāgrat, the common creation shared by all the knowers). The states are the descent of the Lord through the forms of the world.
c1_V3N-one-lord-many.md

The tattvasaṅgraha (the collection of the essence) opens with the single great claim: the own-self alone of all beings is the one Lord, the maheśvara. His re-recollection — "I, this" — is un-broken. But then how does the many arise? In the own-self, by the Lord's freedom, a "this-part" is created, preceded by a contraction; and by the this-ness of the distinct-known, an "I-being" shines, the grasper. He who says "I am happy," grasping himself as this contracted being — that is the bound one. And his liberation is precisely the recognition of what he truly is.
c1_V3O-bond-liberation.md

The bound one's creation is *un-common* (asādhāraṇī) — private, per-knower, per-moment, vanishing with him — yet sustained by the Lord's creation (īśasṛṣṭyujīvinī). The whole difference of bound and liberated hangs on one fact: the bound one does not *know* his own power; he forgets that the world he builds is built with the Lord's own materials. The construction-action is the bond — by it the māyā-power binds the animal; even the "free" constructions ("I, the king, stand") are other-dependent. And there is a path out: the abandonment of construction. When the bound one comes to the "I-this" of the Lord, his animal-ness is destroyed and the Lord-ness shines.
c1_V3P-lover-union.md

The closing sum of the IPVV. The teaching comes from the self, the śāstra, and the guru; the book-studied knowledge without the guru-order is sterile. And its path is the recognition: since liberation is from the recognition alone, the elaborate effort-yogas are useless here; this is the clear means, effort-less, yet bearing the great fruit. Its fruit is the jīvanmukta — the one liberated while still living.  The lover-image states how this is so. The lover stands near, sought by the slender woman, but as long as he is not recognized, he cannot be enjoyed. So the world-Lord, always present, always near, is not experienced in his own splendor until the recognition arises. Recognition does not bring the Lord; it turns the un-known nearness into the joy of union. And because the recognition is an event to be occasioned, not a proposition to be believed, the teaching must come from the guru — the book without the line is sterile.  The passage establishes the recognition as the path and the jīvanmukta as its fruit. Whether the "effort-less" means excludes all practice is a further question the tradition addresses elsewhere.
